entry.dc:title: Brackish Water in Unsaturated Confining Beds at a Texas Lignite Mine
entry.dc:creator: Dutton A.R.
entry.dc:description: Deposits of low permeability are hydrologic barriers between reclaimed land and juxtaposed aquifers and should limit the impact of mining on ground‐water quality. Clay‐stone and mudstone in argillaceous facies of the Calvert Bluff Formation (lower Eocene, Wilcox Group) function as confining beds in the East Texas Basin. In the subsurface and at the outcrop, water in argillaceous deposits is brackish to saline. Samples of vadose water from the outcrop of confining beds at the Big Brown lignite mine in Freestone County, Texas, have a chloride concentration of up to 3,500 mg/l and total dissolved solids of up to 8,000 mg/l. Ground‐water composition evolved from Eocene sea water by seven‐ to nine‐fold dilution with rain water. Ion exchange, pyrite oxidation, and calcite dissolution further modified water composition. The amount of recharge through the vadose zone where confining layers crop out is probably negligible over an extremely long time. Meteoric flushing in reclaimed land at the surface mine is many times greater than that in unmined mudstone deposits, and the chemical composition of vadose water in reclaimed land is changed by further dilution and water‐rock reactions. entry.dc:title: Results of a tree species trial on a recontoured surface mine in southwestern Virginia.
entry.dc:creator: Torbert J.L.
entry.dc:description: Five pine and 10 hardwood species were planted on a reclaimed, return-to-contour, strip-mine site. A systemic herbicide was sprayed on half of each of 4 experimental blocks prior to the 2nd growing season. After 3 growing seasons, this treatment resulted in increased survival of black locust Robinia pseudoacacia (90% survival and a 10-fold increase in height), black alder Alnus glutinosa, sycamore Platanus occidentalis and cottonwood Populus deltoides. As a group, the pines outperformed the hardwoods. Loblolly Pinus taeda and Virginia pine Pinus virginiana were the fastest growing; survival of each was significantly higher on the sprayed plots.-from Authors

entry.dc:title: Systematic variation of iron disulfide occurrences in the Permo- Pennsylvanian Waynesburg coal at a surface mine near Morgantown, West Virginia.
entry.dc:creator: King H.
entry.prism:publicationName: 9e Congres International De Stratigraphie Et De Geologie Du Carbonifere Washington Et Champaign Urbana 1979 Compte Rendu Vol 4
entry.dc:description: The abundance, size, shape, and maceral association of the iron disulfide minerals within the Waynesburg coal were studied. At the mine of study, the coal appears in two 1.5 m-thick benches. Pyrite was the most abundant iron disulfide mineral in the upper bench; marcasite was the most abundant one in the lower bench. Microscopically, iron disulfide occurrences were classified into five categories: 1) framboids, 2) euhedral aggregates, 3) isolated euhedra, 4) cleat and fracture fillings, and 5) irregular shapes. Framboids, euhedral aggregates, and isolated euhedra were the dominant morphologies in the upper bench; irregularly shaped marcasite dominated the lower bench.-from Authors

entry.dc:title: Comparative techniques used to evaluate Thematic Mapper data for land cover classification in Logan County, West Virginia ( USA).
entry.dc:creator: Brumfield J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Landsat 4 Science Characterization Early Results Vol 4 Applications Symposium Greenbelt February 1983
entry.dc:description: Several digital data processing techniques were evaluated in an effort to identify and map active/abandoned, partially reclaimed, and fully revegetated surface mine areas in the central portion of Logan County. The TM data were first subjected to various enhancement procedures, including a linear contrast stretch, principal components and canonical analysis transformations. At the same time, 4 general procedures were followed to produce 6 classifications as a means of comparing the techniques involved. Preliminary results show that various feature extraction/data reduction techniques provide classification results equal or superior to the more straightforward unsupervised clustering technique. -from STAR, 23(13), 1985

entry.dc:title: Potential Effects on Ground Water of a Hypothetical Surface Coal Mine in Indiana
entry.dc:creator: Banaszak K.
entry.dc:description: The possible mine will remove a gently, less than 50 feet per mile, westerly dipping Springfield coal from an area covered by glacial till and some channel sands and gravel. The area is flat, with less than 20 feet of relief in a square mile. The channel sands and gravels, the till and the bedrock are capable of yielding ground water at 5 to 75,3 to 10, and 1 to 10 gallons per minute (gpm), respectively. The ground water in the drift and the shallow bedrock is calcium‐bicarbonate type, contrasting with the sodium‐bicarbonate type in the deep bedrock. The surface mine will feature selective handling of overburden. The probable hydrologic consequences of the mine will be 1) a short‐term, areally limited dewatering, 2) an increase in dissolved solids, 3) a change in ground water chemistry in some areas to a calcium‐bicarbonate sulfate water, 4) an increase in ground water storage, and 5) a new integrated surface water system. The proposed ground water monitoring system will include seven monitoring wells in the glacial material and one in the bedrock. The primary effort in ground water monitoring to the west of the mine will be to detect changes in the quality of the ground water, whereas to the east, changes in both quality and quantity will need to be monitored intensively. entry.dc:title: Final comparison of TM and MSS data for surface mine assessment in Logan County, West Virginia.
entry.dc:creator: Witt R.
entry.prism:publicationName: Landsat 4 Science Investigations Summary Proc Vol 2 1983
entry.dc:description: A variety of classifications during both raw and transformed MSS and TM data sets from September 4, 1982 were performed for the Logan County, West Virginia study area. The object was to compare the utility of TM and MSS data for delineating small, irregular ground features, particularly surface mines, and also to test data reduction/transformation techniques (band selection, canonical analysis, and principal components) in relation to a traditional means of unsupervised classification. Statistical results demonstrate that, on the average, the TM classifications yielded an overall 0.53 factor of improvement.-from STAR, 22(20), 1984

entry.dc:title: APPRAISAL OF THE CORRECT TRANSPORT SYSTEM FOR A SURFACE MINE.
entry.dc:creator: Bullivant D.
entry.dc:description: In general, the objective of any mining operation is to extract the ore from the ground and transport it to the process plant at the minimum cost. It can be argued that the winning of the ore does add value to the product, but certainly the transportation aspect is only a pure cost factor and therefore must be achieved in the most economic way. Off-road trucks represent a very flexible means of handling material within a surface mine and this feature has made them the most widely-used method of transportation.

entry.dc:title: Habitat use by Red-tailed Hawks in surface-mined areas
entry.dc:creator: Mindell D.
entry.dc:description: Habitat use by 4 radio-tagged red-tailed hawks (Buteo jamaicensis) was monitored during 708 transmitter-days in coal surface-mined areas in northern West Virginia and southwestern Pennsylvania in 1977 and 1978. Mean cumulative home range size for the 3 adults was 316.8 ha (3.2 km<sup>2</sup>). Red-tailed hawks showed significant (P<0.005) tendencies to elect certain habitats over others. Descending order of habitat electivity was: 1) woods edge with open area not surfacemined. 2) woods edge with surface-mined area. 3) deciduous woods, 4) open area not surface-mined, and 5) surface-mined area. Red-tailed hawks' flexibility in niche requirements allowed them to exploit reclaimed area. Recommendations for surface mine reclamation are given. © 1984 Science and Technology Letters.

entry.dc:title: DESIGN OF SURFACE MINE BLASTS - A MICROCOMPUTER PACKAGE FOR FIELD USE.
entry.dc:creator: Ghose A.K.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
entry.dc:description: In the search for optimum design of surface mine blasts, several empirical and computer models have been proposed. The paper examines the outline of an interactive model which utilizes theoretical as well as empirical relationships to arrive at an optimum design strategy. An interactive microcomputer package developed for field application is reported.

entry.dc:title: Influence of wetlands and coal mining on stream water chemistry
entry.dc:creator: Kelman Wieder R.
entry.dc:description: Comparisons of stream water chemistry over a 2 yr period in East Fork, which drains an entirely forested watershed, and Big Run, which drains a forested watershed 8 % of which is occupied by Big Run Bog, indicated that Big Run Bog had no effect on stream water H<sup>+</sup> or Cl<sup>-</sup> concentrations, but with increasing stream discharge the wetland was a source of Ca<sup>++</sup> Mg<sup>++</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup>, NO<inf>3</inf><sup>-</sup>, and SO<inf>4</inf><sup>-</sup>, and a sink for Fe<sup>+ +</sup>. Further comparisons with Tub Run, which drains a forested watershed, 13 and 12% of which is occupied by Tub Run Bog and an abandoned, unreclaimed coal surface mine, respectively, suggested that Tub Run Bog removes H<sup>+</sup>, Ca ++, Mg<sup>++</sup>, Fe<sup>++</sup>, and 50<inf>4</inf><sup>-</sup> from inputs of acid mine drainage. Wetland areas on the landscape contribute to the regulation of stream water chemistry in ways that are different from upland areas, and wetlands may have considerable applied potential for minimizing the impact of the mine drainage on stream water quality. © 1984 D. Reidel Publishing Company.

entry.dc:title: HYDROGEOCHEMICAL ASPECTS OF SURFACE MINE RECLAMATION IN THE NORTHERN GREAT PLAINS.
entry.dc:creator: Groenewold G.H.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Society of Agricultural Engineers
entry.dc:description: Studies of several coal-mining sites in western North Dakota have resulted in the development of a hydrogeochemical model which accounts for the observed chemical characteristics of subsurface water in undisturbed settings. Critical hydrogeochemical processes include sulfide oxidation, gypsum precipitation and dissolution, carbonate mineral dissolution and cation exchange. The hydrogeochemical model is equally applicable to undisturbed and spoils landscapes and that the major species of concern in this region are sodium and sulfate. This research indicates that the major source of sulfate is sulfides in the overburden and that the solubility of sulfate in groundwater in these settings is largely controlled by the sodium/calcium ratio.

entry.dc:title: The Environmental Impacts of Surface Mine Development in the Hunter Region of New South Wales
entry.dc:creator: Dragun A.K.
entry.dc:description: Surface coal mining portends to change forever the very economic, as well as environmental fabric, of the Hunter region of NSW. While the benefits of coal mining are substantial, the actual expenditure on surface mine rehabilitation are inconsequential in both absolute and operating terms. Whereas the performance of the existing rehabilitation program is questionable, a range of long term rehabilitation problems threaten profound environmental damage. In this setting the state government would do well to consider the cost impacts of surface mining on other sectors of the community within the region. © 1984, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Aggregation of surface mine soil by interaction between VAM fungi and lignin degradation products of lespedeza
entry.dc:creator: Rothwell F.
entry.dc:description: The external mycelium of a vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhizal (VAM) fungus was effective in aggregating a sandy loam minesoil. The polysaccharide nature of the soil binding agent on hyphal surfaces and on the surfaces of sand particles in contact with the hyphae within the aggregate was demonstrated with the periodic acid-Schiff reagent staining reaction. A possible stabilizing mechanism for macroaggregates was proposed that involves a coupling reaction between glucosamines in the hyphal walls of the fungus with phenolic compounds released during lignin degradation of sericea lespedeza root tissue. © 1984 Martinus Nijhoff/Dr W. Junk Publishers.

entry.dc:title: Within-Tree Distributions and Seasonality of Immature Stages of the Bronze Birch Borer, Agrilus Anxius (Coleoptera: Buprestidae)
entry.dc:creator: Loerch C.R.
entry.dc:description: Distributions of immature stages of the bronze birch borer, Agrilus anxius Gory (Coleoptera: Buprestidae), infesting young European white birch, Betula pendula Roth, were studied on a surface mine reforestation site in Pennsylvania. Eggs of A. anxius were common on boles of trees from mid-June through mid-August, in clusters of up to 14 eggs. Almost 70% of the eggs were in crevices in the dark triangular patch at branch origins. Larvae were present throughout the year. Fourth instars comprised 93.1% of the overwintering population. Vertical distributions of eggs, larvae, and pupae along the bole were random relative to available surface area. Consequently, each stage was more abundant on the lower half than on the upper half of trees. Eggs and first instars were concentrated on the northeast, or shaded, side of trees. Second and third instars were distributed randomly around the bole. Fourth instars overwintered and pupated primarily on the south-west aspect. © 1984, Entomological Society of Canada. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: ROCK REINFORCEMENT DESIGN FOR SURFACE MINE BENCH INSTABILITIES.
entry.dc:creator: Seegmiller B.
entry.dc:description: Horizontally stratified lithologies of certain open pit or strip mines create unique stability problems for mine operations. Slope instabilities may occur when a sandstone unit overlies a shale unit and ground water drains into the mine along the lithologic contact. Large sandstone blocks fail in a toppling mode and cause safety and cleanup problems. Use of rock reinforcement including chain link fencing, roof bolt mats, rock bolts, rock anchors, and shotcrete offers a possible solution.

entry.dc:title: CROSS-PIT SPREADER SELECTED BY COMPUTER FOR NEW SURFACE MINE.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: The Texas lignite fields are becoming receptive ground for innovative mining schemes. North American Coal Corp. is considering using a team consisting of bucketwheel excavators and cross-pit spreader to strip upper strata at one of the two pits at a new multi-seam mine to be located on a 38,000-acre tract east of Dallas. A large-scale software program was used to select the cross-pit spreader for this surface mine.

entry.dc:title: Derivation of a diggability index for surface mine equipment selection
entry.dc:creator: Scoble M.
entry.dc:description: This paper reports on research aimed at developing techniques to predict the influence of ground conditions on excavating equipment performance. The work was conducted in operating British surface coal mines and presents a technique for diggability assessment in that mining and geotechnical environment. A diggability index is proposed which consideres both ground conditions and excavating equipment capabilities. This is supported by reference to back-analysis of several mine excavating case studies. © 1984.

entry.dc:title: WIDCO'S PROGRAM FOR UCG COMMERCIALIZATION.
entry.dc:creator: Paul R.
entry.dc:description: This paper describes the Tono Project, WIDCO's underground coal gasification (UCG) technology development program which is, a phased series of laboratory, field laboratory, and increasingly larger field tests leading to a commercial development. This unique approach to the commercialization of the UCG technology centers around the controlled retracting injection point (CRIP) gasification system. The Tono Project was intiated in 1979 to assess the potential for developing the unminable coal resources of the state of Washington via the UCG technology. Phase I of the program was to determine the role of the UCG in the total development of a coal resource through a total economic coal utilization (TECU). The second phase of the program was to identify potential sites within the Washington where a successful commerical-scale UCG development might be established. The third phase was to identify site-specific conditions which effect the UCG process at the Tono test site through a site characterization study conducted by Sandia National Laboratory. This paper describes the programmed full-scale field gasification test experiment which will be operating by 1986. The first commercial modules would be installed from the coal face exposed at the base of the final highwall in the surface mine, and would access and recover the coal from the area designated as the buffer zone.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE COAL MINING - AN APPROACH TO PRIME FARMLAND REQUIREMENTS.
entry.dc:creator: Sorrell S.
entry.dc:description: To obtain a negative determination for prime farmlands in its approved lignite surface mine permit application, Phillips Coal Co. conducted a soils mapping and historic land use survey. In addressing the justification for topsoil substitute materials, the company relied on results of a geochemical evaluation to demonstrate improved drainage, trafficability, and fertility. The reclamation plan incorporated these elements plus indicator species, existing vegetation, and wildlife needs.
